sugestoes.texto: Create records a failed unified-storage write into the legacy histogram via `recordLegacyDuration`, so any unified-storage error inflates the legacy latency/error metric (label `kind`) even though legacy was never touched. Use `recordStorageDuration(true, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startStorage)` on this storage-error path.

Update records a failed unified-storage update into the legacy histogram via `recordLegacyDuration`, misreporting a storage failure as a legacy failure. Use `recordStorageDuration(true, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startStorage)` here.

The async legacy `DeleteCollection` goroutine records into the storage histogram via `recordStorageDuration`, so legacy delete-collection latency/errors are counted as storage operations and storage metrics are double-counted. Use `recordLegacyDuration(err != nil, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startLegacy)`.

The successful Delete path passes the object `name` as the argument that feeds the `kind` metric label, while the error path on line 103 passes `options.Kind`; this pollutes the `kind` label with object names and makes the two paths inconsistent. Pass `options.Kind` as done on line 103.

The async legacy update is passed the raw `objInfo` instead of a wrapper carrying the object already persisted to the unified store; every other mode (mode2.go:298, mode1.go:244-250) and the previous mode-3 implementation wrapped it in `&updateWrapper{upstream: objInfo, updated: obj}`. Without the wrapper, `Legacy.Update` calls `objInfo.UpdatedObject` against the legacy store's own base object, so for PATCH/merge updates the legacy copy can end up different from the unified-store result. Restore the `updateWrapper` so both stores apply the same computed object.

Delete installs `d.Log` (the base logger) into the context instead of the request-scoped `log` built on line 96, so the `name`, `kind`, and `method` fields are dropped from the logger that `Storage.Delete` and `Legacy.Delete` receive. Use `klog.NewContext(ctx, log)` so downstream logs keep the request context.

The async legacy write derives its timeout from the request-scoped `ctx` (`context.WithTimeoutCause(ctx, ...)`), but the HTTP handler returns immediately after launching the goroutine and the apiserver cancels the request context at that point, so the legacy write races cancellation and is often aborted before it runs. This silently defeats the legacy dual-write safety measure (the same pattern exists in Update line 135, Delete line 110, and DeleteCollection line 163); detach from the request context (e.g. `context.WithoutCancel(ctx)` / a fresh background context) for these fire-and-forget writes.

The async legacy Delete no longer logs failures: the previous implementation called `log.Error(errLS, "could not delete from legacy store")`, but the new goroutine only invokes `recordLegacyDuration` and discards the error, so legacy delete failures become invisible in logs. The same logging removal occurred in Create, Update, and DeleteCollection; re-add a `log.Error` on the goroutine error to preserve the lost observability.

issues.descricao: Delete puts the base d.Log instead of the enriched per-call logger into the context, so downstream logs lose name/kind/method fields.
issues.textoGolden: The context is being created with d.Log instead of the log variable that was initialized with additional context values (name, kind, method). This means those values won't be propagated to the logging context.

comentarios.texto: `ctx = klog.NewContext(ctx, d.Log)` installs the mode-level logger instead of the request-scoped `log` built on line 96 (which carries name, kind and method) — a copy/paste error, as every other method in this file passes the composed `log`. Storage.Delete and the legacy delete goroutine therefore log without the per-request fields this PR is adding (and without the metrics method/kind context).
ctx is built with klog.NewContext(ctx, d.Log) instead of the enriched `log`. The delete logs then lose the name, kind and method values. Use `log`.
The Delete context uses d.Log rather than the per-call log. This is a logging-context inconsistency (not a data leak); use the per-call logger for consistency.

issues.descricao: The legacy DeleteCollection goroutine records its duration with recordStorageDuration instead of recordLegacyDuration, misattributing legacy latency and errors to the storage metric.
issues.textoGolden: In DualWriterMode3's DeleteCollection method, when a storage operation fails, recordStorageDuration is incorrectly called with recordLegacyDuration instead.

comentarios.texto: The legacy DeleteCollection duration and error status are recorded in the unified-storage histogram. Every successful unified deletion therefore produces a second storage observation for a different backend, while legacy deletion failures are attributed to unified storage and no legacy observation is emitted. Call recordLegacyDuration here instead.

The timed call is d.Legacy.DeleteCollection, but its measurement is emitted using recordStorageDuration. Use recordLegacyDuration; otherwise storage receives two measurements for a successful collection deletion and legacy receives none, and legacy failures appear as storage failures.
The legacy DeleteCollection duration is recorded with recordStorageDuration, so legacy latency and errors are attributed to storage. Use recordLegacyDuration.

issues.descricao: Delete's success path records the storage metric with the object name in the kind label instead of options.Kind, creating per-object series and inconsistent labels.
issues.textoGolden: Inconsistency: using name instead of options.Kind for metrics recording differs from other methods.

comentarios.texto: The Delete success-path metric passes `name` where every other call site in this file (lines 48, 103, 113, 156, 159) passes options.Kind in the kind/name argument slot. The storage-success sample for Delete is thus labelled with the object name instead of the resource kind, breaking label consistency with the other operations and with the error sample emitted at line 103. Use options.Kind here (or insert name consistently everywhere, matching the metric's label semantics).
recordStorageDuration(false, mode3Str, name, method, startStorage) at line 106 passes the object name in the kind label slot.

recordStorageDuration is called with the object `name` as the `kind` label: `d.recordStorageDuration(false, mode3Str, name, method, startStorage)`. Every other storage call site passes `options.Kind` (lines 73, 89, 103, 156, 159). This injects a per-object value into the kind label, corrupting the metric and giving it unbounded cardinality (one series per object name), which grows memory on every delete. Should be `options.Kind`.

issues.descricao: On storage Create/Update failure the duration is recorded with recordLegacyDuration, attributing unified-store errors to the legacy metric.

comentarios.texto: On a Storage.Create failure the code records the error with recordLegacyDuration(true, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startStorage) — the failing subsystem is Storage, not Legacy, and it passes the storage start time. This records storage failures under the legacy metric, corrupting the dual-writer error dashboards (and contradicts the success path on line 48 which uses recordStorageDuration). Use d.recordStorageDuration(true, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startStorage).

On a Storage.Update failure the code records the error with recordLegacyDuration(true, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startStorage), attributing a storage failure and its storage duration to the legacy metric. This is inconsistent with the success path on line 132 (recordStorageDuration) and with mode1's semantics. Use d.recordStorageDuration(true, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startStorage).

The async goroutine performing the LEGACY DeleteCollection measures it with d.recordStorageDuration(err != nil, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startLegacy). Every other legacy write in this file uses recordLegacyDuration (lines 56, 113, 140); recording it under the storage metric reports legacy latency/errors as storage latency/errors. Use d.recordLegacyDuration(err != nil, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startLegacy).

issues.descricao: Mode 3 legacy writes now run in background goroutines derived from the request context, which is cancelled when the request completes, so legacy writes can be cancelled and legacy storage falls out of sync.

comentarios.texto: The async legacy write goroutine derives its context from the request-scoped `ctx` (context.WithTimeoutCause(ctx, ...)). The apiserver cancels that context as soon as the HTTP handler returns — which is immediately after Create/Update/Delete/DeleteCollection return — so the goroutine's Legacy.Create can be canceled before completing, silently dropping the legacy write that this mode exists to guarantee. The same applies to the goroutines at lines 108-114, 134-141 and 161-167. Detach the async context from request cancellation (e.g. derive from context.WithoutCancel(ctx) / context.Background()) before applying the timeout.

The legacy write in Mode 3 became fire-and-forget, changing the contract callers relied on: previously Create (and, identically, Update/Delete/DeleteCollection) returned only after the LegacyStorage call had been made in-request; now it returns immediately and the write runs in a detached goroutine. Worse, the goroutine builds its context from the request-scoped `ctx` (line 51: `context.WithTimeoutCause(ctx, ...)`), which the API server cancels as soon as the handler returns/flushes the response — so the legacy write and its 10s timeout will typically be cancelled outright and the legacy store silently stops being updated, which is precisely what the new mode-3 integration cases assume still happens. Any detached work must be given a context not tied to the request lifetime (e.g. context.WithoutCancel(ctx) or a server-lifetime context), and consumers that depended on the synchronous legacy write need to be updated.

The asynchronous legacy write derives its timeout context from the request context, which is canceled when the HTTP request finishes. Create, Update, Delete, and DeleteCollection return before this work completes, so their legacy database operations can be canceled immediately instead of receiving the intended ten-second window. Derive the bounded background context from context.WithoutCancel(ctx) to retain request values without inheriting request cancellation.

issues.descricao: Legacy.Update now receives the original objInfo instead of a wrapper carrying the object stored in unified storage, so legacy recomputes the update and can diverge.

comentarios.texto: Legacy.Update receives the original objInfo instead of the object successfully committed to unified storage. The playlist legacy implementation calls objInfo.UpdatedObject(ctx, old) against its own legacy object, so a patch is reapplied to potentially stale state and can persist a different result or fail rather than mirror the unified write. Pass an updateWrapper containing res, as the previous implementation did.

Legacy.Update previously received an updateWrapper containing the object returned by Storage.Update; it now receives the original objInfo. UpdatedObjectInfo can compute an update from the old object supplied by each backend (notably for patches), so evaluating it against a stale legacy object can produce a different result or reject an update that already succeeded in Storage. Preserve the canonical-result contract by passing an updateWrapper with updated: res and upstream: objInfo to the legacy consumer rather than replaying the original update against legacy state.

Legacy.Update now receives the original objInfo rather than the updateWrapper containing the object successfully committed to Storage. UpdatedObjectInfo can represent a patch/transform based on the supplied old object; replaying it against legacy's potentially different old state can persist a different result or fail, even though the authoritative update succeeded. Restore forwarding of the committed result via updateWrapper instead of recomputing the update against legacy state.

issues.descricao: The Mode 3 tests never wait for or assert the asynchronous legacy writes, and legacy and storage share one mock, so removing the legacy calls would not fail them.

comentarios.texto: The legacy half of Mode 3 is never verified, so these tests cannot catch its removal. Mode 3 is documented as writing to BOTH LegacyStorage and Storage, and the implementation performs the legacy write in a detached goroutine (`go func(){ d.Legacy.Create(...) }()`, dualwriter_mode3.go lines 50-57, and likewise at 108-114, 134-141, 161-167). Each test registers legacy expectations (`setupLegacyFn`, e.g. lines 30-32 and 40-42) but never calls `m.AssertExpectations(t)`, `AssertCalled` or `AssertNumberOfCalls`, and never waits for or observes the goroutine — no channel, no polling. Additionally `legacyStoreMock{m, l}` and `storageMock{m, s}` (lines 53-54, and the same pair in every other test function) share one `*mock.Mock`, so even a count assertion could not distinguish a legacy call from a storage call. Deleting every `d.Legacy.*` call from the implementation leaves all six tests passing, which is exactly the regression the names — and the Mode 3 contract — claim to cover.

The successful Create test never verifies the legacy write. Configuring m.On("Create", ...) does not require that expectation to be consumed, and these assertions only inspect the object returned by Storage.Create. Deleting the entire legacy-create goroutine would still pass this test. Use distinct storage and legacy mocks and synchronize on the legacy call, then assert that it completed with the intended object.

The successful Update case configures a legacy Update expectation but returns after checking only the unified-store result. It neither waits for the asynchronous legacy update nor verifies its expectation, so removing the legacy-update goroutine entirely still passes. Add explicit synchronization and verification of the legacy update (ideally with separate mocks), including the object propagated to legacy storage.

issues.descricao: The List error test case is still named 'not implemented' although List is now implemented and the case checks storage error propagation.

comentarios.texto: The test-case name "error when listing an object in the unified store is not implemented" still describes the old stub List (which returned nil, nil with a "List not implemented" log). List is now implemented at dualwriter_mode3.go:79 and delegates to Storage.List; the case merely checks that a Storage error is propagated. The name contradicts the code it now exercises — rename it, e.g. "error when listing objects in the unified store fails".

issues.descricao: The Create test case name says 'only in the unified store' although Mode 3 also writes to legacy.

comentarios.texto: The test name says creation happens "only in the unified store", but this case configures a successful Legacy.Create as well, and Mode3.Create launches that legacy write after the unified write succeeds. Rename the case to describe creation in both stores (with the legacy write asynchronous), so test output does not communicate the opposite of the mode-3 write contract.

issues.descricao: Independent per-request goroutines remove ordering between legacy writes to the same resource, so legacy can end up with an older version or a resurrected object.

comentarios.texto: Independent goroutines remove ordering between successful writes to the same resource. For example, Storage commits update A and then update B, but the legacy goroutine for B can finish before A, leaving legacy with A while Storage contains B. Likewise a delete can run before an earlier create and leave a resurrected legacy object. Preserve per-resource commit order for mirroring (including across create/update/delete), rather than launching each write independently.

issues.descricao: The storage-failure Create test registers its failing expectation via setupLegacyFn and only works because legacy and storage share one mock.

comentarios.texto: The 'error when creating object in the unified store fails' case registers the failing Create expectation only through setupLegacyFn. It passes only because legacy and storage share one mock, so the storage Create gets that error by accident. Register the expectation in setupStorageFn and use separate mocks for legacy and storage, so the test really covers a storage failure.

issues.descricao: DualWriterMode3.Delete now returns on any unified-storage error, including NotFound, before deleting from legacy, so objects that exist only in legacy can no longer be deleted.
Mode 3 legacy-storage write errors (create/update/delete/delete-collection) are no longer logged after moving to async goroutines; only a duration metric with an error flag is recorded.

sugestoes.texto: When the `use-table-widget-visualization` flag is enabled the table branch renders `TableWidgetVisualization` with hardcoded `columns={[]}` and `tableData` of `{data: [], meta: {fields: {}, units: {}}}`, ignoring `result.data`/`result.meta`. Enabling the flag therefore replaces the real table with an always-empty one, hiding all dashboard table data. Pass the actual `result.data`/`result.meta` (and resolved columns) into `TableWidgetVisualization`.

`validate_timestamp` and `validate_age` test presence with truthiness (`self.initial_data.get("age")` / `.get("timestamp")`) rather than key membership. Because `age` has no `min_value` and `timestamp` permits `0`, a report containing both `age: 0` and `timestamp` (or `timestamp: 0` plus `age`) bypasses the mutual-exclusion check even though the two fields must not co-exist. Use `"age" in self.initial_data` / `"timestamp" in self.initial_data` so both fields are always rejected when present together.

`fetch_error_details` pairs `error_ids` positionally with `events.values()` via `zip`, but `nodestore.get_multi` does not preserve request order. When a replay's error nodes are a mix of cached and uncached entries, cached entries are appended after the uncached ones (`items.update(cache_items)` in nodestore/base.py:205) and ids are deduplicated (line 184), so each `ErrorEvent` gets the wrong `event_id` for its data and the `is not None` filter can silently drop an id. Look up by node id instead — iterate `zip(error_ids, node_ids)` and read `events.get(node_id)`.

When the `use-table-widget-visualization` flag is enabled, `tableResultComponent` renders `TableWidgetVisualization` with hardcoded empty `columns={[]}` and `tableData={{data: [], meta: {fields: {}, units: {}}}}`, discarding the real `result.data`/`result.meta`. Enabling the flag replaces every dashboard table with an empty grid, so the branch must pass the actual `result` data and derived columns rather than empty placeholders.

`validate_timestamp`/`validate_age` test presence with truthiness (`self.initial_data.get("age")` / `.get("timestamp")`), so a falsy value such as `age: 0` or `timestamp: 0` is treated as absent and the mutual-exclusion check is bypassed. Use a membership test (`"age" in self.initial_data` / `"timestamp" in self.initial_data`) so fractional-second and 0 timestamps are validated.

`makeTraceItemAttributeKeysQueryOptions` builds the request without `environment`, whereas the previous `useTraceItemAttributeKeys` sent `environment: selection.environments` to `/trace-items/attributes/`. As a result attribute keys are now fetched across all environments regardless of the selected page filter, returning keys/values not scoped to the user's environment selection. Thread the selected environments through the options object.

issues.descricao: The age/timestamp mutual-exclusion validators check truthiness via initial_data.get(), so a zero value is treated as absent and a report carrying both fields passes validation.
issues.textoGolden: Validation logic incorrectly uses .get('timestamp'), which treats a timestamp of 0 as absent. It should directly check 'timestamp' in self.initial_data to ensure proper field presence detection, preventing both 'age=0' and 'timestamp' from passing mutual-exclusion validation.

comentarios.texto: The timestamp/age validators test truthiness and make both fields optional instead of enforcing exactly one field. Reports with both age=0 and timestamp=0, or with neither field, pass validation despite violating the stated mutually exclusive report formats. Enforce field presence and exclusivity in object-level validate using key membership rather than truthiness.

Check key presence rather than truthiness when enforcing age/timestamp mutual exclusion. Both fields permit 0, so a report with age=0 and timestamp=0 passes both validators even though both fields are present; a zero-valued counterpart also bypasses the corresponding check. Use `"age" in self.initial_data` and `"timestamp" in self.initial_data` (or object-level validation) and add zero-value tests.

Check field presence rather than truthiness when enforcing timestamp/age exclusivity. A report containing both `timestamp: 0` and `age: 0` passes both validators, despite the declared constraint that they must not coexist; with only one zero value, validation is also asymmetric. Use membership checks on initial_data (or object-level validation) and add zero-value mixed-field tests.

issues.descricao: The validation-failure warning logs the entire raw, attacker-controlled browser report instead of a redacted subset.

comentarios.texto: The new validation-failure warning logs `raw_report`, the full unvalidated report object supplied by the caller. This endpoint is public and unauthenticated (permission_classes = (), @csrf_exempt), so the payload is attacker-controlled, and browser report bodies routinely carry sensitive values (CSP blocked-uri/document-uri/script-sample, sourceFile, plus the full user_agent). Logging the raw payload on every validation failure writes potentially sensitive data into application logs; log only the report `type` (or a sanitized/redacted subset) instead of the entire raw object.

Do not attach the complete raw report to the validation warning. Browser reports contain page URLs (potentially including tokens or personal data in query strings) and arbitrary body contents. Any invalid field now causes that entire payload to be emitted at warning level, exposing it in operational logs even where the existing info-level request logging is filtered out. Log the failed field names/report type or a redacted diagnostic instead.

issues.descricao: fetch_error_details pairs error_ids positionally with nodestore get_multi values, but get_multi does not preserve input order (cached items are appended last) and drops missing nodes, so error details get attached to the wrong error IDs.
issues.textoGolden: Using zip(error_ids, events.values()) assumes the get_multi result preserves the input order; dict value order is not guaranteed to match error_ids, so event data can be paired with the wrong ID (missing nodes also shift alignment).

comentarios.texto: WHAT: fetch_error_details zips error_ids with events.values() instead of mapping by node_id, misaligning ids to payloads and dropping/mismatching on missing keys. WHY: assigns wrong title/message/timestamp to wrong error id and yields incorrect Seer logs. HOW: look up each node_id in the get_multi dict (e.g. dict keyed by node_id) and preserve error_ids order.

`zip(error_ids, events.values())` assumes `nodestore.backend.get_multi(node_ids)` values preserve input order and that all keys exist. Dict values give no such guarantee; missing keys shorten/misalign the zip, attaching the wrong event payload to the wrong error_id. Lookup per-id: iterate node_ids/error_ids and do `events.get(node_id)` instead of zipping with `.values()`.

fetch_error_details pairs IDs to payloads with zip(error_ids, events.values()) where events is dict from nodestore get_multi. Values order need not match IDs and missing keys misalign, attaching wrong title/message to wrong error. Look up per node_id instead.

issues.descricao: The Snuba replay lookup for error IDs runs even when enable_error_context=false, adding a needless query (and failure point) to opt-out requests.

comentarios.texto: The new Snuba replay lookup executes even when enable_error_context=false. Every opt-out summary request incurs an unnecessary database round trip and can now fail on Snuba availability even though it only needs recording storage. Evaluate the flag first and perform the replay lookup only when error context is enabled.

issues.descricao: With the use-table-widget-visualization flag on, the widget renders TableWidgetVisualization with hardcoded empty columns and data instead of the query results, so every table widget shows an empty table.
issues.textoGolden: Hardcoded empty data passed to TableWidgetVisualization causes it to always render an empty table instead of displaying actual results when the feature flag is enabled.

comentarios.texto: WHAT: the `use-table-widget-visualization` branch renders `<TableWidgetVisualization columns={[]} tableData={{data: [], meta: {fields: {}, units: {}}}} />`, hardcoding empty rows and no columns instead of the actual query result. WHY: when the feature flag is enabled for an org, every table widget renders an empty table and silently drops `result.data`/`result.meta`/`columns`, a functional regression for all dashboard table widgets. HOW: build `columns`/`tableData` from the existing `result` (and `widget.queries[i].fields`/`fieldAliases`) rather than the empty placeholder objects.

In the new feature-flagged branch, TableWidgetVisualization is rendered with hardcoded empty props: columns={[]} (an empty array, which is truthy for the `columns ?? fallback` logic, so no columns are derived) and tableData={data: [], meta: {fields: {}, units: {}}}. All the real result data computed above (result.data, result.meta, fields, fieldAliases, eventView) is discarded, so any organization with 'use-table-widget-visualization' enabled gets an empty table instead of the query results. Pass the actual result data/columns into the visualization (or keep the old StyledSimpleTableChart) until the widget is properly wired.

With the 'use-table-widget-visualization' feature enabled, TableWidgetVisualization is rendered with columns=[] and empty data/meta instead of result.data and result.meta. Every table widget therefore renders empty for orgs with the flag. Fix: pass tableData={{data: result.data, meta: result.meta}} and build columns from the fields.

issues.descricao: The custom cell renderers fall back to default rendering on any falsy return (0, '', null), not only undefined, so a renderer cannot render zero or an empty cell.

comentarios.texto: The documented custom-renderer contract says fallback runs when the callback returns undefined, but `if (cell)` also falls back for valid ReactNode results such as `0`, an empty string, or `null`. A caller trying to render zero or deliberately suppress a cell instead gets the default field rendering. Check `cell !== undefined` here and in the head-cell renderer so the implementation honors the advertised contract.

Use `cell !== undefined` instead of `if (cell)` to select the custom renderer result, and apply the same correction to the header renderer. The API documents undefined as the fallback sentinel, but valid ReactNode results such as numeric 0, an empty string, or null are falsy. A custom renderer returning 0 or intentionally hiding a cell with null therefore unexpectedly renders the default value instead.

issues.descricao: The attribute-keys query key no longer includes the organization slug, so two organizations with the same filters share a cache entry and switching orgs can show the previous org's attribute names.

comentarios.texto: The new attribute query key omits the organization even though its query function fetches an organization-specific endpoint. Switching organizations with identical project selections such as all projects and the same date range reuses the singleton query client's prior organization's attribute metadata, including while the new request refetches. Include organization.slug or organization.id in the query key.

Include the organization slug in this query key. The new useGetTraceItemAttributeKeys implementation fetches `/organizations/${organization.slug}/trace-items/attributes/`, but makeTraceItemAttributeKeysQueryOptions contains no organization identity. Two organizations with identical filters (particularly the default all-project selection) therefore share this cache entry. Switching organizations can display the previous organization's attribute names, and concurrently mounted consumers can reuse a request for the wrong organization. Preserve the organization-specific cache identity that the previous endpoint-based key provided.

Include the organization slug or ID in this query key. The query function fetches `/organizations/${organization.slug}/trace-items/attributes/`, but the key contains only query options. Two organizations with the same project selection (especially the all-projects selection), date range and dataset therefore share a cache entry. Switching organizations can display the previous organization's attributes, and overlapping requests can populate the shared entry with the wrong organization's result.

issues.descricao: The UseTraceItemAttributeBaseProps doc says only LOGS is supported, although the hooks are also used with SPANS.

comentarios.texto: The new shared prop documentation claims the endpoint currently supports only LOGS, but this PR also uses these hooks with TraceItemDataset.SPANS (for example in TransactionNameSearchBar). Update this comment to describe both supported datasets; as written it incorrectly tells callers that a supported and actively used input is unsupported.

issues.descricao: Error event timestamps (seconds) are compared with replay recording event timestamps (milliseconds), so errors are not interleaved chronologically with breadcrumbs.
dedupedYAxes is now just [yAxis], so its name misdescribes the code.

Every paginated breadcrumb-summary request queries the replay and fetches all of its error events from nodestore with no cap, adding latency and memory proportional to the replay's error count on each page.
HIDDEN_ATTRIBUTES is applied only when a search query is present; the no-search early return shows all attributes, so the hidden attributes still appear in the default span attributes view.

The bulk delete test sets max_segment_id to None to cover the new guard in _make_recording_filenames, but it mocks delete_matched_rows, so the guard is never executed and removing it would not fail the test.
BrowserReportSerializer's validate_timestamp/validate_age docstrings claim one of age/timestamp must be present, but the code only enforces mutual exclusion, so reports with neither are accepted.

sugestoes.texto: The public `findMany(findManyArgs)` method was removed and replaced by `getBaseConditions()`, which no longer accepts or forwards the caller's `where`/`select`/`orderBy`/pagination arguments — it returns only the combined auth+filter `Prisma.Sql` fragment. Any consumer that relied on `InsightsBookingService.findMany` to pass extra predicates (or that expected a typed `BookingTimeStatusDenormalized[]` result) now silently loses that filtering/pagination behavior; since this class is exported, external consumers are invisible to static analysis. Provide a replacement that still threads caller-supplied filters and pagination through, or document the hard breaking change.

The auth-only branch of `getBaseConditions` returns the composite authorization condition unparenthesized, but for `org`/`team` scope that condition is a top-level `OR` (built by the reduce at lines 171-174 / 204-207), so the returned `Prisma.Sql` is something like `(A AND B) OR (C AND D)` without an outer group. When a caller concatenates it with another clause using `AND ${baseConditions} AND <filter>` (the exact pattern this codebase uses for raw insights queries, e.g. routing-events.ts:525), SQL precedence binds the appended `AND` only to the last `OR` operand, so the first branch silently ignores the added filter (e.g. a date range) and returns rows it should have excluded. Wrap the returned condition so the method is safe to combine, e.g. return `Prisma.sql`(${authConditions})`` for the auth-only branch (and likewise for the filter-only branch at line 77) so the whole predicate stays grouped regardless of how callers AND it.

Callers that passed extra `where` predicates or pagination now lose that filtering silently, and external consumers of the exported `InsightsBookingService` are invisible to static analysis. Restore a method that threads caller-supplied filters and pagination through `getBaseConditions`, or document the breaking change.

For `org`/`team` scope the auth condition is a top-level `OR`, so a caller appending `AND <filter>` (as in routing-events.ts) binds only to the last operand and the first branch ignores the filter. Wrap the returned `Prisma.Sql` in parentheses in the auth-only and filter-only branches.

issues.descricao: In getBaseConditions, the branches for a missing authorization condition are unreachable because getAuthorizationConditions always returns a Prisma.Sql.
issues.textoGolden: In getBaseConditions(), the else if (filterConditions) and final else branches are unreachable. This is because getAuthorizationConditions() always returns a non-null Prisma.Sql object, making authConditions always truthy, which means only the first two if/else if conditions are ever evaluated.

comentarios.texto: getAuthorizationConditions() always returns a non-null Prisma.Sql, so the `else if (filterConditions)` and final `else` branches (returning NOTHING_CONDITION) in getBaseConditions can never execute. Simplify to: if filterConditions, combine it with authConditions; otherwise return authConditions.

Unreachable branches in getBaseConditions: authConditions is always a truthy Prisma.Sql object (never null, NOTHING is `1=0`), so `else if (filterConditions)` and final `else { return NOTHING }` can never execute. Simplify to if(filter) return auth AND filter else return auth, or make the nothing-case explicit.

WHAT: `getBaseConditions` returns `filterConditions` alone (no authorization predicate) when `authConditions` is falsy (`else if (filterConditions) { return filterConditions; }`). sugestoes.texto: Each flusher process now builds its own `SpansBuffer(shards)` holding only a subset of shards, but `flush_segments` derives `max_segments_per_shard = ceil(max_flush_segments / len(self.assigned_shards))` from that subset, so every process independently fetches up to ~`max-flush-segments` per cycle. The documented cap `spans.buffer.max-flush-segments` ('Maximum number of segments to fetch and flush per cycle') is therefore applied once per process, making the effective global limit `max_flush_segments * num_processes` and multiplying in-flight memory/CPU per cycle. To keep the cap global, divide the budget by the total number of processes (e.g. pass the total shard count/factor into the per-process buffer) or scale `max_flush_segments` down by `num_processes`.

`get_memory_info()` returns cluster-wide memory for every Redis node regardless of `assigned_shards` (`iter_cluster_memory_usage` in backpressure/memory.py ignores shards), yet `submit` now calls it once for every per-process buffer and concatenates the results. This issues N redundant full-cluster INFO round trips per submit (N = number of flusher processes) and duplicates every node entry. Since the used/available ratio is unchanged and only one buffer per distinct client is needed, call `get_memory_info()` once (e.g. on a single buffer or the shared client) instead of looping over `self.buffers`.

`_create_process_for_shard` (singular) was added but has no callers anywhere in the codebase — grep finds only its definition, and the restart logic in `_ensure_processes_alive` uses `_create_process_for_shards` (plural). This dead helper suggests a shard-level restart path that is never actually exercised, so a per-shard restart intent (restart only the process owning a given shard) is silently unreachable. Either wire it into the restart flow or remove it.

When the join deadline is already exhausted at the start of an iteration, the `break` (lines 340-341) exits the loop before reaching `process.terminate()`, so that process and every subsequent flusher worker are neither waited on nor terminated. The previous single-process `join` always called `terminate()` after the wait, so with multiple flusher processes and a `timeout`, a hung/worker process can survive `join()` and keep flushing to Kafka/Redis during rebalance. Move the `terminate()` into a finally/continue path (or terminate each process before breaking) so every process is stopped regardless of remaining deadline.

issues.descricao: The restart path only kills a hung flusher if it is a multiprocessing.Process, but spawn-context workers are SpawnProcess, so hung processes are never killed and a duplicate flusher is started for the same shards.
issues.textoGolden: Because flusher processes are created via multiprocessing.get_context('spawn').Process, they are instances of multiprocessing.context.SpawnProcess, which on POSIX is not a subclass of multiprocessing.Process, so this isinstance check will always be false and hung processes won't be killed here.

comentarios.texto: The new isinstance(process, multiprocessing.Process) guard does not match the SpawnProcess instances created by self.mp_context.Process. When a worker hangs, the guard skips kill() and the replacement starts while the original worker remains alive, allowing overlapping flushing of the same shards if the original resumes and leaking hung workers. Check against multiprocessing.process.BaseProcess or self.mp_context.Process, and kill and join the old worker before replacing it.

The workers are created with get_context("spawn").Process, which produces SpawnProcess instances; these are not instances of multiprocessing.Process (the default-context Process class). Consequently this guard skips kill() for actual production workers. When a worker hangs, the replacement starts while the original remains alive and can resume flushing the same shards. Use multiprocessing.process.BaseProcess or the spawn-context Process class for the check, and fix the identical check in join() so shutdown also terminates surviving workers.

Workers created by multiprocessing.get_context("spawn").Process are SpawnProcess instances, not instances of the separate multiprocessing.Process class. Consequently this guard skips kill() for production workers. When a live worker exceeds max-unhealthy-seconds, the code starts a replacement and overwrites its handle while the original is still running. If the original resumes, both workers flush the same shards, and repeated hangs can exceed the configured process limit. Check against multiprocessing.process.BaseProcess (or explicitly distinguish threads) and stop the old worker before replacing it.

issues.descricao: join() breaks out of the per-process loop when the shared deadline expires, skipping termination of the remaining flusher processes and leaving them running after shutdown.
issues.textoGolden: Breaking out of the loop when the deadline has elapsed can skip terminating remaining flusher processes, potentially leaving them running after shutdown; consider ensuring termination is attempted even if the deadline is exceeded.

comentarios.texto: join() breaks out of the worker loop when the shared deadline expires, skipping cleanup for every remaining worker. If next_step.join consumes the timeout or an earlier worker exhausts it, remaining flushers can continue running after shutdown or partition reassignment. Use the deadline only to limit waiting and still terminate and reap every remaining process.

Do not break out of worker cleanup when the join deadline expires. If the first worker consumes the timeout, the next iteration breaks before terminating that worker or any subsequent workers. They may still be blocked in Redis or producer calls despite the shared stopped flag, leaving old workers running after strategy shutdown/reassignment. Apply the deadline only to waiting, and perform termination cleanup for every worker regardless of remaining time (using a type check that recognizes spawn-context workers).
join() waits for processes sequentially against a single shared deadline and breaks without terminating remaining processes once it expires, leaking them.

comentarios.texto: The docstring says the flusher "Creates one process per shard for parallel processing," but the code at lines 60-66 shares shards across a capped number of processes (num_processes = min(self.max_processes, len(buffer.assigned_shards)); each shard assigned via i % self.num_processes). With the new --flusher-processes default of 1, a single process handles every shard, so the documented contract is the opposite of the behaviour this PR introduces (confirmed by test_flusher_processes_limit, which asserts 4 shards served by 2 processes). Update the docstring to say shards are distributed across up to max_processes flusher processes.

The new docstring says this creates one process per shard, but workers are capped by max_processes and shards are distributed among them. In particular, the CLI default of 1 means all assigned shards share one process. Describe capped workers with potentially multiple shards per worker so callers do not rely on per-shard process isolation.

The docstring says the flusher 'Creates one process per shard', but the number of processes is capped by max_processes (--flusher-processes), and shards are shared across processes via i % num_processes. Reword it to say that shards are distributed across at most max_processes processes.

issues.descricao: max_processes uses a truthiness fallback, so --flusher-processes 0 silently becomes one process per shard instead of being rejected.

comentarios.texto: `max_processes or len(buffer.assigned_shards)` treats a falsy value as 'not provided'. The new `--flusher-processes` click option is `type=int`, so a user can pass `0`; that legitimate-but-falsy value is discarded and the flusher silently spawns one process per shard instead of honoring the requested limit. Use an explicit None check, e.g. `self.max_processes = max_processes if max_processes is not None else len(buffer.assigned_shards)` (and validate/reject 0 upstream).

An explicit max_processes=0 is treated as an omitted limit by `or`, so passing `--flusher-processes 0` starts one process per assigned shard instead of respecting or rejecting the supplied zero limit. The CLI accepts zero as an integer and the factory forwards it unchanged. Default only when max_processes is None, and explicitly validate that supplied process limits are positive so zero cannot silently enable potentially many workers.

`max_processes or len(buffer.assigned_shards)` uses a truthiness test, so an explicit 0 is treated as 'unset' and silently expands to one process per shard. Use `max_processes if max_processes is not None else len(buffer.assigned_shards)` and reject values below 1.

issues.descricao: A negative --flusher-processes value is not validated and makes SpanFlusher construction fail with KeyError.

comentarios.texto: `flusher_processes` is not validated to be >= 1. `self.max_processes = max_processes or len(buffer.assigned_shards)` lets a negative value through (it is truthy), so `self.num_processes = min(self.max_processes, len(...))` becomes negative and `range(self.num_processes)` is empty, leaving `process_to_shards_map` as `{}`. The following loop computes `process_index = i % self.num_processes`, which for any negative divisor is 0, so `self.process_to_shards_map[0].append(shard)` raises KeyError and the consumer fails to construct. Since `flusher_processes` is exposed as an int CLI option (`--flusher-processes`), a negative value is reachable from configuration. Guard with `max(1, self.num_processes)` / validate the input.
negative max_processes flows through `or` guard into min() -> empty map -> KeyError on i % num_processes; empty assigned_shards yields zero processes.

Fetch cluster memory information once from a single buffer.

sugestoes.texto: The `catch` block increments `retryCount` for every exception thrown anywhere in the try body, not only SMS send failures. Because deletion (lines 38-42) is driven purely by `retryCount > 1`, two transient/unrelated errors (e.g. a `prisma.profile.findFirst` or `getBookerBaseUrl` failure, or the success-path update throwing after a message was actually sent) permanently delete the reminder before a successful delivery ever happens. Increment the counter only when the send itself failed (e.g. around the `twilio.scheduleSMS` call), and rethrow or log unrelated errors without counting them as retries.

The new `OR` branch filters on `retryCount`, which has no index on WorkflowReminder. PostgreSQL cannot use the existing `[method, scheduled, scheduledDate]` index to satisfy an OR with an unindexed column, so this `deleteMany` degrades to a sequential scan of the entire WorkflowReminder table on every cron invocation. Add an index on `retryCount` (or restructure the delete to avoid the OR across an unindexed column) so this cron job stays index-backed as the table grows.

The new `else` branch treats every falsy return from `twilio.scheduleSMS` as a send failure and increments `retryCount`, but `scheduleSMS` returns `undefined` when `isLockedForSMSSending(userId, teamId)` is true (a deliberate skip, not a failure). For an account temporarily locked for SMS sending, each cron tick bumps `retryCount`, and once it exceeds 1 the `deleteMany` permanently deletes reminders that were never actually attempted, so the booking's SMS reminder is lost instead of being deferred until the lock is lifted. Only increment `retryCount` for genuine send errors (e.g. have `scheduleSMS` distinguish the locked case, or check the lock/pending state before updating).

issues.descricao: retryCount is set to reminder.retryCount + 1 from a value read at the start of the run instead of an atomic increment, so overlapping runs can lose increments.
issues.textoGolden: Using retryCount: reminder.retryCount + 1 reads a possibly stale value and can lose increments under concurrency; consider an atomic increment via Prisma (increment: 1) to avoid race conditions (also applies to the similar update in the catch block).

comentarios.texto: WHAT: retryCount is incremented with a read-value computed at the start of the run (`retryCount: reminder.retryCount + 1`) instead of an atomic increment. WHY: if two cron invocations overlap (or the same reminder is processed twice before the write commits), both read the same retryCount and both write N+1, so failures are undercounted and the reminder can loop forever without ever reaching the `retryCount > 1` deletion threshold. HOW: use `data: { retryCount: { increment: 1 } }` so the increment is atomic (the initial read value is then irrelevant).

`retryCount: reminder.retryCount + 1` is a read-modify-write of the value fetched at the top of the handler, not an atomic increment. Two overlapping cron runs both read the same retryCount and both write the same +1, losing an update, so failed reminders can be retried indefinitely and never reach the `gt: 1` deletion threshold. Use Prisma's atomic `retryCount: { increment: 1 }` instead of computing from the stale in-memory value (same issue in the else branch at lines 179-186).

Retry counts are assigned from the stale findMany snapshot instead of incremented atomically, both here and in the catch branch. Two overlapping cron requests can each fail scheduling the same reminder with retryCount zero and both write one, so two failed attempts do not reach the deletion threshold and additional attempts are scheduled. Use Prisma's atomic retryCount increment operation in both failure branches.

issues.descricao: The deleteMany OR clause applies retryCount > 1 without the SMS method filter, so the SMS cron deletes any workflow reminder (email, WhatsApp) with retryCount above 1.
issues.textoGolden: The deletion logic in scheduleSMSReminders.ts incorrectly deletes non-SMS workflow reminders (e.g., Email, WhatsApp) that have retryCount > 1. This occurs because the retryCount condition within the OR clause for deletion lacks a method: WorkflowMethods.SMS filter, causing it to apply to all reminder types instead of only SMS reminders, which is the intended scope of this function.

comentarios.texto: The comment "//delete all scheduled sms reminders where scheduled date is past current date" no longer describes the deleteMany below it. After this change the query also deletes reminders with retryCount > 1, and that OR branch has no `method: WorkflowMethods.SMS` filter, so non-SMS (email) reminders with retryCount > 1 are now deleted too. Update the comment (or add the missing SMS filter to the retryCount branch) so the prose matches what the code actually deletes.
The deleteMany OR clause deletes any reminder with retryCount > 1 regardless of method.

The second OR branch `{ retryCount: { gt: 1 } }` has no `method` filter, unlike the first branch (`method: WorkflowMethods.SMS`). Because `retryCount` is a generic column on WorkflowReminder used by all reminder methods, this deleteMany now permanently deletes every reminder of ANY method (including EMAIL) whose retryCount exceeds 1, even though this cron is only supposed to clean up SMS reminders. Add `method: WorkflowMethods.SMS` to this branch (or scope the whole where to SMS) so non-SMS reminders are never destroyed.

issues.descricao: The cleanup comment describes only past-date SMS deletion and omits the new retryCount > 1 deletion branch.

comentarios.texto: Update the cleanup comment to describe the new retry-exhaustion deletion branch. It currently says this deletes scheduled SMS reminders whose date has passed, but this OR branch also deletes any reminder with retryCount > 1, including future-dated reminders and without an SMS restriction. The comment now misrepresents the scope of this destructive operation.

Stale comment: line 28 says 'delete all scheduled sms reminders where scheduled date is past current date' but the new OR clause also deletes any reminder with retryCount > 1 regardless of method or date. Update the comment to describe both branches.

issues.descricao: The retry-count update inside the catch block is not guarded, so if it throws (for example the reminder was deleted concurrently) the error escapes the loop and the cron run fails, skipping the remaining reminders.

comentarios.texto: WHAT: the catch block performs an unguarded `prisma.workflowReminder.update` while handling the scheduling error. WHY: if this write itself rejects (e.g. the row was concurrently removed, or a transient DB error), the rejection is not caught and escapes the for-loop, aborting the whole cron run so all remaining reminders go unprocessed. HOW: wrap the retryCount update in its own try/catch (log and continue) so a failure to record the retry does not abort processing of the remaining reminders.

This new `prisma.workflowReminder.update` sits inside the catch block, which is NOT protected by any try/catch. If this update throws (e.g. the reminder was already removed by the `deleteMany` at the top of the file during a concurrent run -> Prisma P2025, or a transient DB error), the exception escapes the `for` loop and rejects the handler, so all remaining unscheduled reminders are skipped and the cron request fails. Previously the catch only did `console.log`, so a single bad reminder never aborted the batch and the endpoint always returned 200. Wrap this update in its own try/catch (or `updateMany`/catch-and-log) so a failed retry-count write cannot take down the whole scheduling run.

The new database update inside catch can itself throw when a reminder has been deleted during scheduling. Booking cancellation deletes reminders through handleCancelBooking and deleteScheduledSMSReminder, so a concurrent cancellation followed by a scheduling error now rejects the entire cron handler and prevents the remaining reminders from being processed. Use an updateMany filtered by the reminder ID to tolerate an already-deleted row, and guard errors from retry bookkeeping so they do not escape the per-reminder error handler.

issues.descricao: Claims transient errors increment retryCount, so two runs during an outage delete the whole pending SMS reminder queue.

comentarios.texto: WHAT: The catch block unconditionally increments retryCount for any exception (profile/bookerUrl/templating/rate-limit/Twilio outage). WHY: Two consecutive cron runs with a transient global failure increment every pending SMS reminder to 2 and the startup deleteMany then wipes the entire future SMS queue, not just permanently-invalid numbers. HOW: Only increment on permanent scheduleSMS failure, or distinguish transient errors from terminal ones before counting toward deletion.

issues.descricao: The new OR arm on retryCount has no supporting index, so the cleanup delete can no longer be fully served by the existing index and may scan the table.

comentarios.texto: WHAT: the deleteMany WHERE now uses `OR` between `(method = SMS AND scheduledDate <= now)` and `retryCount > 1`, but WorkflowReminder has no index on the newly added retryCount column. WHY: Postgres cannot satisfy a two-way OR using the existing (method, scheduled, scheduledDate) index and will fall back to a sequential scan of the entire WorkflowReminder table on every cron invocation, turning a previously indexed delete into a full table scan as the table grows. HOW: add an index on retryCount (or restructure so each branch is index-usable), then re-check the query plan.

comentarios.texto: The retryCount increment is duplicated in the else-branch and catch.

issues.descricao: SMS-sending locks are counted as failed scheduling attempts: scheduleSMS returns undefined for locked users/teams, retryCount is incremented, and after two cron runs the retryCount > 1 cleanup deletes future reminders even if sending is later unlocked.

sugestoes.texto: Adding the `organizationId == null || BROKER_PUBLIC` clause to the shared `LoginFilter.getLoginPredicate()` also changes `IdentityProviderBean.federatedProviderPredicate()` (IdentityProviderBean.java:226), which `getFederatedIdentityProviders` uses to decide which of the user's existing federated identity providers can be linked. As a result, any IDP linked to an organization without `BROKER_PUBLIC=true` is now silently dropped from the account-linking list even though that code path is org-unaware and previously accepted it. If the widened predicate is only meant to drive login-cache invalidation, keep the org/BROKER_PUBLIC check local to `InfinispanIdentityProviderStorageProvider` instead of the shared SPI method that the login/account beans reuse.

"alias" is a literal string rather than the actual IDP alias, so none of the created IDPs is ever cleaned up. Use the real alias (e.g. the loop's alias variable / "idp-alias-20") when registering the cleanup. As written, the 21 leaked providers can skew later tests that count IDPs or login caches.

The cleanup is registered for the literal alias "alias" rather than the IDP just created ("idp-alias-" + i). The 20 created IDPs are never removed, and the same applies to the cleanup at line 425 for "idp-alias-20". Use the actual alias, e.g. get("idp-alias-" + i)::remove, so the IDPs don't leak into other tests.

The cleanup registered here uses the literal alias "alias", but the provider just created has alias "idp-alias-" + i. The same mismatch is repeated at line 425 for "idp-alias-20". The cleanup can never find/remove the created providers (null dereference/404 on remove, or at best a silent no-op), so none of the 21 IDPs this test creates are cleaned up and the realm is left polluted for later tests. Use the actual alias, e.g. `testRealm().identityProviders().get("idp-alias-" + i)::remove` and `get("idp-alias-20")::remove`.

issues.descricao: On a partial cache miss getForLogin merges the previously read login query into a newly revisioned entry, so a concurrent invalidation can be lost and stale IDP IDs for other organizations persist.

comentarios.texto: Do not merge the previously read query into a newly revisioned entry without verifying its revision. A reader can obtain a query containing organization A's IDs, then another transaction disables a provider or changes its organization and invalidates this key. When the reader requests an uncached organization B, this branch obtains a fresh revision but copies the old A results into the new query and publishes it using the current counter. Subsequent A requests receive stale membership indefinitely (a disabled or moved provider still exists, so the null-ID fallback does not repair it). Rebuild rather than copy after invalidation, or ensure the old query's revision is still valid atomically before publishing the merged entry.

issues.descricao: Login-cache invalidation on update compares the organization-aware enabled state, so changing a broker to private while its organization is disabled skips invalidation and leaves the now-private IDP in the cached login list.

comentarios.texto: The early return compares the original IDP's organization-aware enabled state rather than the persisted enabled state used to populate the login cache. If a cached public IDP's organization is disabled and an admin changes BROKER_PUBLIC to false, the original predicate is false because the organization is disabled and the updated predicate is false because the broker is private, so the stale ID remains cached; re-enabling the organization displays the now-private broker because the login bean only rechecks isEnabled. Compare raw persisted models for login-cache invalidation, for example by loading the original through idpDelegate.getById before applying this predicate.

issues.descricao: The LoginFilter javadoc still claims its constants are all criteria for login availability although getLoginPredicate now also checks organization link and BROKER_PUBLIC.

comentarios.texto: getLoginPredicate now also filters on organization link plus the BROKER_PUBLIC config (line 254), but the enum's javadoc directly above (lines 215-217) still states that the enum "contains all fields that are considered when deciding if a provider should be available for login or not", presenting ENABLED/LINK_ONLY/HIDE_ON_LOGIN as the exhaustive criteria. Any reader — or a future LoginFilter constant added against that documented assumption — will believe organization link and BROKER_PUBLIC play no role. Update the javadoc to include the organization-link/public-broker condition, or move the condition into a documented LoginFilter constant.

issues.descricao: The test never consumes or asserts getForLogin's returned providers and never repeats a query, so the cache-hit path that builds the result is untested and could return wrong IDPs without failing.

comentarios.texto: Consume and assert the results of getForLogin, including a repeat query for the same mode/organization to exercise a cache hit. All calls in this test discard the returned stream and assert only IdentityProviderListQuery contents. The implementation populates that query before reconstructing the returned models, so returning an empty stream (or the wrong providers) at line 254 would still pass the entire test. Assert the expected provider identities on both the initial query and the cached query, rather than only the internal cached count.

sugestoes.texto: `queued: datetime = timezone.now()` evaluates `timezone.now()` once at class-definition (import) time, so every `AssignmentSource` instance carries the identical, stale module-import timestamp instead of its own creation time. Any future consumer using `queued` for ordering, TTL, or debounce would silently get wrong values; use `field(default_factory=timezone.now)` so each instance captures its creation time.

issues.descricao: AssignmentSource.queued defaults to timezone.now() evaluated at class definition, so all instances share the import-time timestamp instead of the time they were queued.
issues.textoGolden: The AssignmentSource dataclass uses queued: datetime = timezone.now() as a default field value, which evaluates timezone.now() once at class definition time and shares that single datetime instance across all objects.

comentarios.texto: WHAT: `queued: datetime = timezone.now()` evaluates once at class-definition time so every AssignmentSource without explicit queued shares the same timestamp. WHY: queued time is wrong/stale for all later instances and defeats its purpose as a queue-time marker. HOW: use `field(default_factory=timezone.now)` (with `field` import).

Field `queued: datetime = timezone.now()` is evaluated once at import so all AssignmentSources share the same timestamp. Use `field(default_factory=timezone.now)` so each instance measures its actual creation/queue time.

The dataclass field default `queued: datetime = timezone.now()` is evaluated a single time when the module is imported, so every AssignmentSource created without an explicit `queued` value (which is exactly what `from_integration` does, and what `from_dict` falls back to when the key is absent) shares the same frozen import-time timestamp instead of the moment the assignment was actually queued. This makes the `queued` timestamp semantically wrong/meaningless (it reflects process start, not assignment time) and would silently misreport the queue time anywhere this value is later inspected. Fix by defaulting in a factory/`__post_init__` or making the caller pass the timestamp, e.g. set `queued` inside `from_integration` (`queued=timezone.now()`), or use `field(default_factory=timezone.now)`.

sugestoes.texto: `order($val)` passes the same value to `-webkit-box-ordinal-group`/`-moz-box-ordinal-group`, but those legacy properties are 1-indexed (default `1`) whereas `order`/`-ms-flex-order` are 0-indexed (default `0`), so the prefixed and standard declarations disagree on the item's position. Any consumer that relies on the default position (e.g. an `order(1)` item sitting beside an un-ordered sibling) will be ordered incorrectly in legacy WebKit/Gecko; add 1 when emitting the ordinal-group properties (`$val + 1`) so the fallbacks match `order`.

issues.descricao: The flex-item styles target the inner .extra-info-wrapper instead of the component's root div, so in the flexbox header a long topic title keeps its full width and pushes the navigation panel out instead of being truncated.

comentarios.texto: The flex-item styling targets the inner .extra-info-wrapper rather than the outer div generated by header-extra-info's Ember.Component. With .contents now using flexbox, that outer div retains its automatic minimum width, so a long nowrap topic title cannot shrink to the available space and pushes the navigation panel outside the header instead of being ellipsized by the existing desktop truncation rules. Move the extra-info-wrapper class onto the component's root element and set min-width: 0 on that flex item so ordering and truncation apply to the actual header child.

issues.descricao: The align-items mixin emits no -moz-box-align, so on old Firefox versions using the display:-moz-box fallback the advertised vertical centering is not applied.

comentarios.texto: The alignment mixin does not match the Mozilla fallback emitted by flexbox(): when display: -moz-box is selected, neither align-items nor the WebKit/MS declarations control its cross-axis alignment. Consequently @include align-items(center) in the header and small-action leaves those children at the legacy default instead of vertically centering them. Emit -moz-box-align: $alignment alongside -webkit-box-align so the advertised fallback produces the same alignment.

issues.descricao: The align-items mixin emits -ms-align-items, which never existed in IE/Edge; the legacy property is -ms-flex-align, so the declaration is dead.
issues.textoGolden: -ms-align-items never existed in any version of IE/Edge; the correct legacy property is -ms-flex-align.

comentarios.texto: WHAT: align-items() mixin emits -ms-align-items: $alignment which is not a valid IE10/11 property (only -ms-flex-align exists). WHY: dead declaration shows wrong contract and leaves IE alignment dependent solely on -ms-flex-align, which also breaks for flex-start/flex-end values. HOW: remove the -ms-align-items line and map flex-start/flex-end to start/end for -ms-flex-align/-webkit-box-align.

Further this PR removes the float-based right alignment for .d-header .panel, which may cause the login panel in the non-Ember/noscript header (where .panel is nested inside .row and not a flex item) to stack under the title instead of remaining right-aligned.
